readings.title: The shop that received parcels
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: Pine Valley's village shop became a parcel collection point. Drivers made fewer repeat trips, but customers arrived during the shop's busiest food-shopping hour. The owner introduced a separate collection shelf and displayed quieter suggested times while keeping normal access available. She also arranged authorised collection by a nominated neighbour for residents who could not travel. The service succeeded because it fitted local routines, not simply because parcels could be stored in a room. Each convenience created work that had to be planned, and the shop recorded that work before agreeing to expand.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

readings.title: A route drawn from experience
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A new rural driver followed navigation software into a narrow lane that was unsuitable for the delivery van. After the incident, experienced drivers contributed notes about weak bridges, seasonal flooding and safe turning places. Dispatchers kept the digital route planner but checked its suggestions against the local notes. The notes included dates so that temporary restrictions would not remain indefinitely. Neither source was treated as perfect. Combining a broad map with current local knowledge made planning more reliable, especially on roads that general navigation systems rarely assessed in detail.

readings.title: The message before the journey
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A delivery company sent a standard message saying a parcel would arrive 'today'. For residents who worked in distant fields, this required waiting at home for many hours. The company began sending a narrower estimated window and a second message when the driver reached the previous stop. Weather and road conditions could still change the estimate, so the message explained that it was not a guarantee. Residents could also choose collection at the depot. Better communication did not make every journey predictable, but it allowed people to arrange their day with less unnecessary waiting.
knowledgePoints: 阅读：主旨、细节、推断与语境词义

readings.title: Packaging returned on the next trip
readings.instruction: Read the original simulation passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content: A rural cooperative tested reusable delivery boxes. Customers could return an empty box with their next order, but some ordered only a few times a year. Boxes then remained unused in homes for months. The cooperative added return points at two village shops and offered a smaller deposit refund there. More boxes came back into circulation. Staff still inspected and cleaned each one. Reuse depended not just on a durable container but on a convenient return system. Counting boxes delivered would have exaggerated success if most had never been used again.

translation.stem:
Translate the following original passage into Chinese. Preserve the meaning and logical relationships.

Delivering goods to a rural area involves more than covering a long distance. A driver must consider road conditions and whether someone will be available to receive a parcel. A shared collection point can reduce repeated journeys. Its opening hours, however, must suit the people it serves.
translation.referenceAnswer: 向乡村地区配送货物并不仅仅意味着走很长的路。司机还必须考虑路况，以及是否有人能够收取包裹。共享取件点可以减少重复行程，不过它的开放时间必须适合所服务的居民。
translation.explanation: 参考译文仅示范一种表达。评分时关注信息完整性、转折和条件等逻辑关系；意思准确且中文自然的其他译法同样有效。

writing.stem:
Write an English response of about 120 words to the following original simulation task. Use your own examples and organise your ideas clearly.

Write a proposal for a village parcel collection point. Explain its benefits, operating hours and arrangements for residents who cannot travel easily.
writing.sampleAnswer: I propose a parcel collection point in the village shop. It could reduce repeated delivery journeys and allow residents to collect orders when they are already shopping. Opening hours should include at least two early evening periods for people who work elsewhere. The shop would need a secure storage area and a clear process for checking collection details. Residents unable to travel could nominate a trusted neighbour, with authorisation recorded before collection. The organisers should also measure the time staff spend on the service, since convenience creates work as well as benefits. A three-month trial would help the village assess demand and adjust the arrangements before expanding. The service should fit local routines instead of expecting everyone to change them.
